First, is the overall approach correct? The write-up uses a spiral similarity at A sending B to C, M to N. Wait — does a spiral similarity centered at A sending B to C also send M to N? M is the midpoint of AB, N is the midpoint of AC. A spiral similarity centered at A with ratio AC/AB sends B to C. It sends M (midpoint of AB) to the midpoint of A and S(B) = midpoint of A,C = N. Yes, since spiral similarity is a complex multiplication (rotation+scaling) centered at A, it's affine and maps midpoints to midpoints. Actually a spiral similarity centered at A is z -> A + λ(z - A) with λ complex. So M = A + (B-A)/2 maps to A + λ(B-A)/2 = (A + C)/2 = N. Correct. So the "Key Geometric Fact" is true.

Lemma 1: S sends ray BA to ray CA. Hmm, wait. S(B) = C. S fixes A. So the ray BA (from B through A) maps to ray C A? The image of ray BA (i.e., ray starting at B going through A) under S is the ray starting at S(B) = C going through S(A) = A, i.e., ray CA. OK. Then they say S sends ray BK to... they want S(K) on ray CL. They compute angle between S(BK) and CA equals angle between BK and BA = α. And angle ACL = α is the angle between CA and CL. "Since both S(BK) and CL start at C and make angle α with CA on the same side..." This is asserted — the "same side" claim is plausible given interiority but the lemma itself has a subtle issue: a spiral similarity with ratio AC/AB and rotation angle BAC sends B to C, and the image of K is somewhere; the claim that S(BK) and CL are the same ray requires that the angle made with CA is the same and they're on the same side. This is at least a plausible lemma; whether it's fully rigorous about orientation is debatable, but roughly OK as an argument.
